summary: James Miller, a scholar in Sinology and religious studies, earned an M.A. from the University of Cambridge (-1997) and a Ph.D. from Boston University (-2000). He served as Professor of Chinese Studies and Religious Studies at Queen's University Belfast (attested 2014).

James Morison was an Indologist who studied at the University of Oxford under Arthur Anthony Macdonell and at the University of Vienna under Georg Bühler (~1891–1893, Ph.D.). He served as Librarian at the Indian Institute, University of Oxford (1914).

James Murdoch worked in Japanology, history, and archaeology. He studied at the University of Aberdeen (~1874–1879) and under Theodor Benfey (~1878–1880). He held posts at the University of Tokyo (~1890–1893), Kanazawa University (~1900–1901), and Kagoshima University (~1901–1908).

James Prinsep worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. He served at the Kolkata Mint (1819, 1830–1838), the Benares Mint (1820–1830), and led The Asiatic Society (1832–1838). He founded the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal and Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum.

James Rennell worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served in the Bengal Engineers (1764) and surveyed Bengal for the East India Company (1764–1777). Later elected to several academies, he founded the Royal Geographical Society in 1830.

James Robert Ballantyne was an Indologist, philosopher, and linguist educated at the University of Edinburgh, Glasgow (Ph.D.), and East India Company College under James Michael and Francis Johnson. He led Benares Sanskrit College (1845–1861) and later worked at King's College London and East India House.

James Robson is a scholar of Buddhist studies, Sinology, and religious studies who earned his BA at UC Santa Barbara and PhD at Stanford. He held posts at Williams College, University of Michigan, and Harvard University, becoming director of the Harvard-Yenching Institute in 2024.

James Roland Ware specialized in Sinology, Buddhist studies, and Indology. He studied at the University of Pennsylvania under Franklin Edgerton and under Sylvain Lévi. He held posts at Lehigh University (1924), the University of Washington (~1926–1927), and Harvard University (1932–1934).

James Smith Reid, a historian and archaeologist, studied at the University of Cambridge (~1865–1869). He held academic posts at Christ's College, Cambridge (1869–1880), Pembroke College (1873–1885), and Gonville and Caius College (1878–1926).

James Stark was active in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as a Puisne Justice of the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka in 1840 and as President of the Royal Asiatic Society of Sri Lanka in 1845.

James Stewart King was a scholar in Iranian and Central Asian studies, history, and archaeology. He completed his education at Trinity College Dublin and the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst (~1866–1868).

James Sutherland Cotton was active in Indology, history, and archaeology. After studying at Trinity College, Oxford (1867–1870), he served as a Fellow and Lecturer at Queen's College, Benares, and held a post at Queens' College (1871–1874).

James Taft Hatfield was a scholar of linguistics and Indology who studied at Northwestern University and Johns Hopkins (Ph.D. ~1887–1890). He served as Professor of Classical Languages at Rust College (1884–1885) and as Professor at Northwestern University (1890–1934).

James Talboys Wheeler worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as Professor of Moral and Mental Philosophy at Presidency College, Chennai (~1860–1862), and later as Assistant Secretary to the Government of India (~1862–1870).
James Thomas Molesworth was an Indologist and linguist. He served as a linguist with the Bombay Native Infantry in 1814 and also held a position as a linguist in the Commissariat Department.

James Tod worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He studied at the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich, and under Gyanchandra. He served with the East India Company (~1798–1826) and as Librarian of the Royal Asiatic Society (~1823–1835).

James W. Benson is a scholar in Indology and linguistics. He held posts as faculty at Harvard University (attested 1999), at the University of Oxford (attested 1999), and at Wolfson College, Oxford (attested 2001).

James W. Heisig, a scholar in philosophy, religious studies, and Japanology, earned degrees from Divine Word College, Loyola, Notre Dame, and Cambridge. He was a longtime Permanent Research Fellow at Nanzan University and served at the Nanzan Institute for Religion and Culture (~1978–2020).
James Ward was a philosopher who studied at Fitzwilliam College (~1869–1872) and Trinity College, Cambridge (~1872–1875). He later held an academic post at the University of Cambridge (~1897–1925).
James Whitehill was a scholar in Buddhist studies, religious studies, and philosophy. He served as Professor of Religion at Stephens College (attested 2000) and founded the Columbia Zen Center.
